message.content:
Lions (Panthera leo) and zebras (Equus quagga) do not share a recent common ancestor in the sense of a single, named species. Instead, their most recent common ancestor lies deep in the tree of placental mammals, at the base of the **Laurasiatheria** super‑order.

- **Kingdom:** Animalia  
- **Phylum:** Chordata  
- **Class:** Mammalia  
- **Infraclass:** Eutheria (placentals)  
- **Superorder:** Laurasiatheria  

Within Laurasiatheria, the lineage that led to modern carnivores (including lions) split off from the lineage that led to perissodactyls (including zebras) sometime during the late Cretaceous period, roughly **70–80 million years ago**. This hypothetical ancestor would have been a small, generalized mammal—perhaps similar in size and ecology to other early eutherians of the time—but it is not known as a distinct species because it predates the fossil record for many of its descendants.

So, the common ancestor of lions and zebras is a **Laurasiatherian mammal that lived about 70–80 million years ago**, rather than a specific, identifiable species.

Zebras: Kingdom Animalia > Phylum Chordata > Class Mammalia > Infraclass Eutheria > Superorder Laurasiatheria > Order Perissodactyla > Family Equidae > Genus Equus > Species quagga.

So both are in the superorder Laurasiatheria. That includes orders like Artiodactyla (even-toed ungulates), Cetartiodactyla, Perissodactyla (odd-toed ungulates), Chiroptera (bats), Carnivora, etc. So the common ancestor would be at the level of Laurasiatheria.
